svg.text: Rotary Phone → Pico (RP2040) — Rev G (replaces GP10 PWM/transistor receiver driver with a MAX98357A I2S DAC+amp module, 2026-07-26)
Dial fully isolated from phone network. WHITE = shunt/off-normal (N1), BLUE = pulse (N2), GREEN/WHITE = switchhook lever (N3), RED/BLACK = carbon mic (N4), WHITE/GREEN = receiver (N5).
Every dashed box below is a component that physically lives inside the phone (handset or dial); everything outside the dashed boxes is the discrete circuit you are building on/around the Pico.
Phase 0 DMM result: mic resistance ~0.5–2kΩ baseline, drifting with ambient sound, spiking 5kΩ+ on shock — confirms carbon mic. Receiver (earpiece) ~50–300Ω electromagnetic coil.

Rev G rationale: revF's bare-transistor PWM driver had no gain stage (Q1 only switches the rail through the coil) -- max output was a few mW, audibly "barely there" even at full duty swing. MAX98357A is a real Class-D amp with true gain, driven over I2S (hardware DMA, no MicroPython real-time bottleneck).
Pin.PULL_UP enabled in software (GP3, GP4 only)
under the handset cradle — GREEN/WHITE pair (N3)
No PWM carrier, no flyback diode, no DC-block cap needed —
the MAX98357A's bridged Class-D output is already AC (zero
average DC across OUT+/OUT-), so it drives the coil directly.
Verify the receiver's actual DCR with a DMM: if it's much
higher than the ~4-8Ω speaker load this chip expects (a
vintage coil often is), volume will still be current-limited —
but the chip's real gain + 5V bridged swing should still beat
the old bare-transistor driver by a wide margin.

S3 is a true dry contact (DMM confirmed: ≈0Ω pressed, open released), same as BLUE. Internal Pin.PULL_UP on GP4 is sufficient; C6 100nF to GND adds EMI immunity for the long handset cord (RC ≈ 5–8ms).
Lever PRESSED (handset resting) = on-hook = GP4 LOW (closed to GND) = MUTE (main.py sends a 0% volume HID report, remembering the last dialed target).
Lever RELEASED (handset lifted) = off-hook = GP4 HIGH (pulled to 3V3) = firmware restores the last dialed volume target automatically.
Debounce: 30ms (heavier lever spring than the dial contacts, which use 15ms). Polarity within the GREEN/WHITE pair does not matter.
Mic + receiver front end — status & next steps (Rev G)
Mic front end (Phase 1) COMPLETE and hardware-verified: bias measured 1.648V, dead-center of the 1.65V target. No changes in Rev G.

Receiver driver (Phase 2) REVISED in Rev G: the bare-transistor PWM driver (GP10/R8/Q1/D1/C5) is superseded by a MAX98357A I2S DAC+amp module -- it has real gain, unlike a plain switch, and offloads audio timing to RP2040 DMA hardware instead of a MicroPython loop.
Any film/polyester/polypropylene caps on hand are fine for C3 (coupling) and C4 (filter); use electrolytic for the bulk C1 (100μF) bias decoupling — film at that value is unnecessarily large.

Next: rewire GP16/17/18 + VBUS/GND to the MAX98357A per this diagram (disconnect the old R8/Q1/D1/C5 stage), rewrite receiver_test.py to use machine.I2S instead of PWM, then re-test tone/melody/PCM playback.
Component hunt list: R4 220–330Ω, R5 4.7k, R6/R7 2×100k; C1 100μF, C2 100nF, C3 1–10μF, C4 10nF, C6 100nF; one MAX98357A breakout module (replaces R8/Q1/D1/C5/general NPN/1N4148 from Rev F).
